items.readable_text:
Content:
Until now, we've been dealing with line integrals with respect to arc length. In this lesson, we will learn about other types of line integral.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: C] is a path in the [MATH: xy]-plane with initial point [MATH: A] and terminal point [MATH: B.] The line integral of the function [MATH: f(x,y)] with respect to [MATH: \boldsymbol x] along the path [MATH: C] is denoted

Content:
[MATH: \int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
To understand what this integral represents, we imagine traversing [MATH: C] from [MATH: A] to [MATH: B.] At each point [MATH: P] that lies on [MATH: C,] we project the point on [MATH: f] that lies directly above [MATH: P] onto the plane [MATH: y=0.] Doing this for every point on [MATH: C] traces out a curve. The line integral of [MATH: f] with respect to [MATH: x] gives the (signed) area bounded by this curve and the [MATH: x]-axis.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a729ecde58816e10ace5265a4c8bb528]

Content:
To calculate a line integral with respect to [MATH: x,] we must first parameterize [MATH: C] using a parameter [MATH: t\in [a,b].] Then, we apply the change of variables formula

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

Content:
Let's take a look at a concrete example.

[IMG: /graphics/4ab0e4cbe6e7788f713bbf2c1f85726e]

Find a definite integral that's equivalent to the line integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_C (x+y) \, \textrm{d} x,] where [MATH: C] is the path along the line segment from the point [MATH: (0,0)] to the point [MATH: (3,3),] as shown above.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We will use the formula [MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

The curve [MATH: C] is a line segment with endpoints [MATH: (0,0)] and [MATH: (3,3).] It can be parametrized as [MATH: r(t)|= ⟨0 + t(3 − 0), 0 + t(3 − 0)⟩; = ⟨3t, 3t⟩,] where [MATH: 0 \le t \le 1.]

Computing [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},] we get the following: [MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(3t) = 3]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = x+y,] we obtain [MATH: f(r(t))|= 3t + 3t; = 6t.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as [MATH: ∫_(C)f(x, y)dx|= ∫_{0}^{1}f(r(t))(dx)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}6t ⋅ 3dt; = 18∫_{0}^{1}tdt.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

We will use the formula [MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

The curve [MATH: C] can be parameterized as [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 5\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

sections.readable_text:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int_C \left(x^2 + y^2\right)\,\textrm d y,] where [MATH: C] is the path along the upper-right quarter of the circle [MATH: x^2 + y^2 = 4,] traversed from the point [MATH: (2,0)] to the point [MATH: (0,2),] as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/b3d9fdb6a6ec0f267a2223a7f1436f91]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We will use the formula

[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

The curve [MATH: C] is a quarter of a circle of radius [MATH: 2] centered at [MATH: O.] It can be parameterized as [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

Computing [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},] we get the following:

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(2\sin t) = 2\cos t]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2], we obtain

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Until now, we've been dealing with line integrals with respect to arc length. In this lesson, we will learn about other types of line integral.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: C] is a path in the [MATH: xy]-plane with initial point [MATH: A] and terminal point [MATH: B.] The line integral of the function [MATH: f(x,y)] with respect to [MATH: \boldsymbol x] along the path [MATH: C] is denoted

Content:
[MATH: \int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
To understand what this integral represents, we imagine traversing [MATH: C] from [MATH: A] to [MATH: B.] At each point [MATH: P] that lies on [MATH: C,] we project the point on [MATH: f] that lies directly above [MATH: P] onto the plane [MATH: y=0.] Doing this for every point on [MATH: C] traces out a curve. The line integral of [MATH: f] with respect to [MATH: x] gives the (signed) area bounded by this curve and the [MATH: x]-axis.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a729ecde58816e10ace5265a4c8bb528]

Content:
To calculate a line integral with respect to [MATH: x,] we must first parameterize [MATH: C] using a parameter [MATH: t\in [a,b].] Then, we apply the change of variables formula

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

Content:
Let's take a look at a concrete example.

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to X

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/4ab0e4cbe6e7788f713bbf2c1f85726e]

Find a definite integral that's equivalent to the line integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_C (x+y) \, \textrm{d} x,] where [MATH: C] is the path along the line segment from the point [MATH: (0,0)] to the point [MATH: (3,3),] as shown above.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the formula
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

The curve [MATH: C] is a line segment with endpoints [MATH: (0,0)] and [MATH: (3,3).] It can be parametrized as
[MATH: r(t)|= ⟨0 + t(3 − 0), 0 + t(3 − 0)⟩; = ⟨3t, 3t⟩,]
where [MATH: 0 \le t \le 1.]

Computing [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},] we get the following:
[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(3t) = 3]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = x+y,] we obtain
[MATH: f(r(t))|= 3t + 3t; = 6t.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as
[MATH: ∫_(C)f(x, y)dx|= ∫_{0}^{1}f(r(t))(dx)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}6t ⋅ 3dt; = 18∫_{0}^{1}tdt.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Line Integrals With Respect to Y

Content:
The line integral with respect to [MATH: \boldsymbol y] of the function [MATH: f(x,y)] along the path [MATH: C] is denoted

Content:
[MATH: \int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d y.]

Content:
This integral represents the total area accumulated when [MATH: f] is projected on the plane [MATH: x=0] as [MATH: C] is traversed from the initial point [MATH: A] to the terminal point [MATH: B.]

Content:
To calculate a line integral with respect to [MATH: y,] we must first parameterize [MATH: C] using a parameter [MATH: t\in [a,b].] Then, we apply the change of variables formula

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.]

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(5\sin t) = 5\cos t]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = x^2,] we obtain

Therefore, we can write the integral as
